zh:
卷第六
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
釋禪波羅蜜修證第七之二
釋四無量心，開為五：第一、明次第；第二、釋名；第三、明處所；第四、明修證；第五、明功德。
en:
Fascicle Six
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding
Explaining Dhyāna-Pāramitā's Cultivation and Realization, Topic 7, Part 2

Explaining the four immeasurable minds: this opens into five parts — first, clarifying their sequence; second, explaining their name; third, clarifying where they are cultivated; fourth, clarifying their cultivation and realization; and fifth, clarifying their merit.

items.en: Why the Immeasurable Minds Follow the Four Dhyānas

zh: 第一、釋四無量心所以次四禪後者，明行人有二種：一者、世間行人；二者、出世間行人。就凡夫行人中，則有三：一者、樂高勝自在，求作梵天王，是故雖得四禪，而更進修無量心。何以故？然四禪但是色界，自行具足，而無益他之德淺薄。若生彼天，不得王領。若修四無量心，緣於十方眾生而入三昧，慈悲普攝，利他心大，是故功德轉多。若生彼天，必作梵天王，王領自在，是故能得四禪，猶更修習四無量心。
en: First, explaining why the four immeasurable minds come after the four dhyānas: this is clarified with reference to two kinds of practitioner — worldly practitioners; and world-transcending practitioners.

Among ordinary, worldly practitioners, there are, in turn, three kinds. First, those who delight in a lofty, sovereign freedom, seeking to become the Great Brahmā King — such a person, although already having attained the four dhyānas, cultivates the immeasurable minds still further. Why is this? Because the four dhyānas alone belong only to the form realm, complete in their own self-cultivation, but shallow and slight in any merit that benefits others. Were one to be born into that heaven on the strength of the four dhyānas alone, one would not thereby rule as its king. But if one cultivates the four immeasurable minds, entering samādhi with the ten directions' own sentient beings as its object, loving-kindness and compassion embracing all universally, the mind of benefiting others thereby made great — the merit is correspondingly far greater. Reborn into that heaven on this strength, one is certain to become the Great Brahmā King, ruling there in sovereign freedom — hence, even having already attained the four dhyānas, one cultivates the four immeasurable minds still further.

zh: 二者、外道行人雖得四禪，而見有心識之患，欲求涅槃無想寂滅，不知破色，直用邪智滅心，入無想定。三者、或有凡夫外道行人悉厭患色，猶如牢獄，一心破色，修四空定，是為凡夫行人同得此定，志樂不同，各隨所習，愛樂不同。若佛弟子，有二種人，所謂小、大兩乘。是二種人得四禪時，進修無量心者，小乘之人為自調心，增長福德，易得涅槃故；大乘之人欲度眾生，必以大悲為本，故次四禪，明修四無量心。
en: Second, non-Buddhist practitioners: although they, too, attain the four dhyānas, they come to see a defect in the very presence of mind and consciousness, and, wishing to seek nirvāṇa as a thoughtless cessation, not knowing how to break through form, simply use a deviant wisdom to extinguish the mind instead, entering the concentration of no-thought.

Third, there are ordinary, non-Buddhist practitioners who grow entirely weary of form, as though it were a prison, and, single-mindedly breaking through form, cultivate the four formless concentrations. These, then, are ordinary practitioners who attain these same concentrations in common, yet whose aspirations and delights differ, each following their own habituation, their own objects of attachment differing from one another.

As for the Buddha's own disciples, there are two kinds of person, namely the two vehicles, lesser and greater. These two kinds of person, upon attaining the four dhyānas, go on to cultivate the immeasurable minds further as well: the practitioner of the lesser vehicle does so in order to regulate their own mind and increase merit, so that nirvāṇa may be more easily attained; the practitioner of the greater vehicle, wishing to liberate sentient beings, must necessarily take great compassion as the very root of this — hence, following the four dhyānas, the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds is now clarified.

zh: 問曰：如《摩訶衍》中假設問云：「是四禪中有四無量及十一切入等諸定，今何故別說？答曰：雖四禪中皆有是法，若不別說，人則不知其功德。譬如囊中有寶，若不示人，即無人知者。若欲示大福德，為說四無量心；患厭色如牢獄，為說四無色定；於緣中不得自在觀所緣，為說八勝處；若有遮道，不得通達，為說八背捨；心不調柔，不能從禪起，次第入禪，為說九次第定；不能得一切緣遍照隨意，為說十一切處。」
en: Question: as the Mahāyāna treatise poses this very question: "Within the four dhyānas themselves, the four immeasurable minds, the ten totality-bases, and other such concentrations are already present — why, then, are they spoken of separately? Answer: although these dharmas are indeed all already present within the four dhyānas, were they not spoken of separately, people would have no way of knowing their own particular merit. It is like a treasure kept within a sack: unless it is shown to someone, no one will ever know it is there. Wishing to display great merit, the four immeasurable minds are spoken of; being troubled by and weary of form as though it were a prison, the four formless concentrations are spoken of; not yet being free and at ease with respect to one's objects in contemplating what is taken as object, the eight stations of mastery are spoken of; where the path is obstructed and cannot be penetrated through, the eight liberations are spoken of; where the mind is not yet pliant and soft, unable to arise from one dhyāna and enter the next in due sequence, the nine sequential concentrations are spoken of; and where one is not yet able to illuminate every object at will, the ten totality-bases are spoken of."

zh: 問曰：若以論說，今得四禪者，亦應悉得四無量等諸禪定否？答曰：此依義而說，若無漏四禪中說有四無量心，則於義無過。何以故？無漏禪中具諸觀行法門故。若有漏根本禪，說者當知乳中說酪耳。
en: Question: if the treatise says this, then should one who has now attained the four dhyānas also be understood to have thereby already attained the four immeasurable minds and the other such concentrations as well? Answer: this is spoken of with reference to a particular sense. If it is the uncontaminated four dhyānas that are said to already contain the four immeasurable minds, this is indeed without fault, since the uncontaminated dhyānas are already complete with every contemplative dharma-gate within them. But if it is the contaminated root dhyānas that are meant, then one should know that this is like speaking of curd as already present within milk.

The three kinds of ordinary practitioner sketched here — the status-seeker aiming for kingship over Brahmā's heaven, the non-Buddhist practitioner who mistakes extinguishing the mind for nirvāṇa, and the practitioner who treats form itself as a prison to escape — quietly set up two false paths (the coming aside on 無想定, deviant no-thought concentration, and the four formless concentrations both trace back to these same motives) against which the properly Buddhist cultivation of the immeasurable minds, and later the formless concentrations, will be contrasted. The milk-and-curd simile is a precise piece of reasoning, and it is applied to the contaminated root dhyānas: to say that they already contain the immeasurable minds is like speaking of curd in milk — true only in a potential sense, with the immeasurable minds still to be separately cultivated. In the uncontaminated four dhyānas, by contrast, which are complete with every contemplative dharma-gate, saying that the immeasurable minds are already present is without fault.

zh: 第二、釋四無量名者：一、慈無量心者，慈名愛念眾生，常求樂事以饒益之；二、悲無量心者，悲名愍念眾生，受五道中種種身苦；三、喜無量心者，喜名欲令眾生從樂得歡喜；四、捨無量心者，捨三種心，但念眾生，不憎不愛。緣此四法故，說於四心，遍十方平等無隔，名無量心。修慈心，為除眾生中瞋覺故；修悲心，為除眾生中惱覺故；修喜心，為除眾生中不悅樂故；修捨心，為除眾生中憎愛故。此四定次第階級之相，在下當釋。
en: Second, explaining the name of the four immeasurable minds: first, the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness — loving-kindness means holding sentient beings in loving regard, constantly seeking what brings them happiness, in order to benefit them. Second, the immeasurable mind of compassion — compassion means holding sentient beings in pitying regard, aware of the various bodily sufferings they undergo across the five realms. Third, the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy — sympathetic joy means wishing sentient beings to attain delight through their own happiness. Fourth, the immeasurable mind of equanimity — equanimity means relinquishing these three preceding states of mind, simply holding sentient beings in mind without either aversion or attachment.

Taking these four dharmas as their object, four states of mind are spoken of, pervading the ten directions equally, without any division between them — hence they are named the immeasurable minds. Cultivating loving-kindness serves to remove the disturbance of anger among sentient beings; cultivating compassion serves to remove the disturbance of vexation among sentient beings; cultivating sympathetic joy serves to remove displeasure among sentient beings; and cultivating equanimity serves to remove aversion and attachment among sentient beings. The mark of these four concentrations' own graduated sequence will be explained below.

items.en: Where the Immeasurable Minds Are Cultivated

zh: 第三、明修處所，自有二種：一、為通明處；二者、別明處。第一、通明處者，四禪、中間定悉得修四無量心，如《釋論》中說：「是慈在色界、根本禪，亦在禪中間。」無色界無色，於緣眾生為不便，欲界、未到地定淺，不任修諸功德。問曰：欲界、未到地，利根之人能用此定發見思真解，何故不得修四無量心？答曰：緣理之慧利，故得發。若神通無量等，是事法，必假深定，而欲界、未到非全不得修無量心，但發得，即屬初禪，是故不說。
en: Third, clarifying where they are cultivated: this itself has two kinds — the general locus; and the particular locus.

First, as for the general locus: the four dhyānas and the intermediate dhyānas are all places where the four immeasurable minds may be cultivated, as the Exegetical Treatise says: "Loving-kindness is present within the form realm's root dhyānas, and within the intermediate dhyānas as well." The formless realm has no form, and so is unsuited to taking sentient beings as an object; and desire-realm concentration and the "not-yet-arrived" state are too shallow to sustain the cultivation of such merit.

Question: practitioners of sharp faculty within the desire realm and the "not-yet-arrived" state are able to use this very concentration to bring forth the true understanding of the path of vision and cultivation — why, then, can the four immeasurable minds not be cultivated there? Answer: it is the sharpness of wisdom directed at principle that allows this to be brought forth there. But supernormal powers, the immeasurable minds, and the like are matters of actual practice, and necessarily depend upon deep concentration; it is not that the desire realm and the "not-yet-arrived" state are entirely incapable of cultivating the immeasurable minds at all, only that, whenever they are brought forth there, they properly belong to the first dhyāna already — hence this is not spoken of separately.

zh: 如初禪五支、覺觀二支分別欲界，則生悲易，喜支生喜易，樂支生慈易，一心支生捨易，故說為修證之處。問曰：第四禪及中間無喜樂，云何以喜樂與眾生？答曰：內雖無有喜樂，緣取外喜樂人相而平等與樂。譬如離欲行人，自不須五塵，亦不與塵欲交染，而為大福德故，亦以五欲勝妙樂具給施前人，而於自心無所染污。於四禪中與他喜樂亦復如是。未到、中間類即可解。
en: As with the first dhyāna's five factors: the two factors of initial thought and sustained reflection, distinguishing the desire realm, make compassion easy to bring forth; the factor of joy makes sympathetic joy easy to bring forth; the factor of happiness makes loving-kindness easy to bring forth; and the factor of one-pointedness of mind makes equanimity easy to bring forth — hence these are spoken of as the proper places for their cultivation and realization.

Question: the fourth dhyāna and the intermediate dhyāna have no joy or happiness at all — how, then, can joy and happiness be given to sentient beings there? Answer: although there is no joy or happiness present within, one takes up the mark of another's outward joy and happiness as one's object, and bestows this happiness equally. It is like a practitioner free of desire, who, having no need of the five sense-objects for themselves, and no longer mingling with or stained by desire for these objects, may nonetheless, for the sake of great merit, still bestow the finest and most excellent pleasures of the five desires upon another person, all without the practitioner's own mind being stained by it in the least. Bestowing joy and happiness upon others within the fourth dhyāna is exactly the same. The "not-yet-arrived" state and the intermediate dhyāna may be understood by the same pattern.

zh: 第二、別明修處者，如初禪以覺觀為主，深識欲界眾生苦惱之相，此處修悲則易。二禪內有大喜，此處修喜無量則易。三禪內有遍身之樂，此處修慈則易。四禪妙捨莊嚴，此處修捨為易。此則隨地各有其便。問曰：若爾，佛何故說住四禪修四無量易得耶？答曰：第四禪名念清淨，得不動定，於此中修一切佛法功德易成，故作是說耳。問曰：上說初禪行悲，此則壞於次第。如慈在前，應初禪而修慈，二禪修悲，三禪修喜，四禪修捨，何故不爾？答曰：此逐義便，不隨次第。譬如佛十弟子各有第一，若問何人智慧第一，應答身子是。若以夏臘大而答第一者，則於義大僻。
en: Second, clarifying the particular locus: within the first dhyāna, initial thought and sustained reflection are its ruling factors, and deeply recognize the desire realm's own sentient beings and the mark of their suffering — hence compassion is easy to cultivate here. The second dhyāna has great joy present within it — hence sympathetic joy is easy to cultivate here. The third dhyāna has happiness pervading the whole body present within it — hence loving-kindness is easy to cultivate here. The fourth dhyāna is adorned with subtle equanimity — hence equanimity is easy to cultivate here. This, then, is a matter of each stage having its own particular convenience.

Question: if this is so, why does the Buddha say that abiding in the fourth dhyāna makes the four immeasurable minds easy to attain? Answer: the fourth dhyāna is named purity of mindfulness, attaining the unmoving concentration — within this stage, every merit of the Buddhadharma is easily accomplished, and so it is spoken of in this way.

Question: it was said above that compassion is practiced within the first dhyāna — does this not disrupt the proper sequence? Since loving-kindness comes first, should not loving-kindness be cultivated in the first dhyāna, compassion in the second, sympathetic joy in the third, and equanimity in the fourth — why is it not so? Answer: this follows whatever is most fitting to the sense at hand, not a fixed sequence. It is like the Buddha's ten chief disciples, each foremost in his own respect: if asked who is foremost in wisdom, the answer should be Śāriputra; but were one to answer according to seniority in ordination instead, this would be a serious error of sense.

The pairing between each dhyāna's own dominant factor and the immeasurable mind it makes "easy" is a genuinely elegant piece of structural matching: initial thought and sustained reflection's raw awareness of others' suffering suits compassion; the second dhyāna's excited joy suits sympathetic joy; the third dhyāna's pervasive happiness suits loving-kindness; the fourth dhyāna's settled equanimity suits equanimity. That this "easy" sequence (compassion, joy, loving-kindness, equanimity) doesn't match the standard naming order (loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity) is explicitly flagged and defended with the Śāriputra example — a reminder, consistent with this treatise's handling of other apparent contradictions, that different orderings can each be correct relative to a different organizing question.

quiz.q: The four immeasurable minds are explained under which five headings?
options: name, marks, sifting the deviant, cultivation, karmic result
expedient, proper practice, factors, substance and function, progress and regression
loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity, no-thought
sequence, name, where cultivated, cultivation and realization, merit
quiz.why: The text opens the topic into five: sequence, name, where cultivated, cultivation and realization, and merit; §2–§9 follow this outline.

quiz.q: Why does the first kind of ordinary practitioner, seeking to become the Great Brahmā King, cultivate the immeasurable minds after attaining the four dhyānas?
options: the four dhyānas cannot lead to the form realm at all
in order to break through form and enter the formless concentrations
the four dhyānas are complete only in self-cultivation, slight in benefiting others; with the immeasurable minds one is certain to rule as Brahmā King
the four dhyānas regress, and the immeasurable minds keep them
quiz.why: The four dhyānas alone are complete in self-cultivation but slight in benefiting others, so rebirth on their strength alone does not make one king. Breaking through form is the aim of the third kind of practitioner.

quiz.q: After attaining the four dhyānas, what do non-Buddhist practitioners see, and what do they do, that leads them into the concentration of no-thought?
options: they see form as a prison and break through it
they see the fault of joy and enter the third dhyāna
they see beings suffer and give rise to great compassion
they see a defect in mind and consciousness and, not knowing how to break through form, use deviant wisdom to extinguish the mind
quiz.why: Non-Buddhists see a defect in mind and consciousness and, not knowing how to break through form, use deviant wisdom to extinguish the mind. Seeing form as a prison describes the third kind, who cultivate the formless concentrations.

quiz.q: Ordinary practitioners attain the same concentrations with differing aspirations. What is the aspiration of the third kind?
options: to liberate beings, with great compassion as root
to become Brahmā King and rule freely
to regulate their own mind and attain nirvāṇa easily
weary of form as a prison, they break through form and cultivate the four formless concentrations
quiz.why: The third kind grow weary of form as a prison and cultivate the four formless concentrations. Seeking Brahmā kingship is the first kind; the last two options describe the Buddha's disciples.

quiz.q: Why do disciples of the lesser and greater vehicles each go on to cultivate the immeasurable minds?
options: the lesser vehicle to regulate the mind, increase merit, and attain nirvāṇa easily; the greater to liberate beings, with great compassion as root
the lesser for Brahmā heaven; the greater for no-thought
both to become Brahmā King
the lesser to break through form; the greater to break through consciousness
quiz.why: The lesser vehicle cultivates them to regulate the mind and increase merit so nirvāṇa is easier; the greater vehicle must take great compassion as the root of liberating beings.

quiz.q: The Mahāyāna treatise asks why concentrations already within the four dhyānas are spoken of separately. What simile answers it?
options: a treasure in a sack: unless shown, no one knows it is there
a clear-water pearl in turbid water
butter within milk
friction-fire gradually burning damp wood
quiz.why: Though these dharmas are present in the four dhyānas, people would not know their merit unless they were spoken of separately, like a treasure in a sack. Butter in milk belongs to the next exchange.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, for one troubled by form as by a prison, which concentrations are taught?
options: the nine sequential concentrations
the four immeasurable minds
the eight liberations
the four formless concentrations
quiz.why: To display great merit, the immeasurable minds are taught; for weariness of form as a prison, the formless concentrations. The eight liberations answer an obstructed path; the nine sequential concentrations, an unpliant mind.

quiz.q: Where the path is obstructed and cannot be penetrated, which dharma does the treatise say is taught?
options: the eight stations of mastery
the eight liberations
the four immeasurable minds
the ten totality-bases
quiz.why: For an obstructed path, the eight liberations. The stations of mastery answer lack of ease in contemplating one's object; the totality-bases answer inability to illuminate every object at will.

quiz.q: Where the mind is not pliant, unable to arise from one dhyāna and enter the next in sequence, which concentration is taught?
options: the four formless concentrations
the eight liberations
the ten totality-bases
the nine sequential concentrations
quiz.why: An unpliant mind that cannot pass from dhyāna to dhyāna in sequence is given the nine sequential concentrations; inability to illuminate every object at will is given the ten totality-bases.

quiz.q: Does one who attains the four dhyānas thereby already have the immeasurable minds and the rest? How does the text answer?
options: whoever attains the four dhyānas has every concentration
only non-Buddhist dhyānas contain them
said of the uncontaminated dhyānas, it is faultless; said of the contaminated root dhyānas, it is like speaking of butter in milk
such a person can never have them
quiz.why: Of the uncontaminated four dhyānas this is faultless, since they contain every contemplative gate; of the contaminated root dhyānas it is only like butter said to be in milk, present potentially.

quiz.q: How does the text define loving-kindness?
options: holding beings in mind without aversion or attachment
holding beings in pity, aware of their sufferings in the five realms
holding beings in loving regard, constantly seeking what brings them happiness, to benefit them
wishing beings to attain delight through happiness
quiz.why: Loving-kindness is holding beings in loving regard and seeking their happiness. The other options define compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

quiz.q: How does the text define compassion?
options: wishing beings the happiness of nirvāṇa
loving regard, seeking their happiness
holding beings in pity, aware of the bodily sufferings they undergo in the five realms
relinquishing the three preceding minds
quiz.why: Compassion is holding beings in pitying regard, aware of the bodily sufferings they undergo across the five realms.

quiz.q: What does the immeasurable mind of equanimity relinquish?
options: body, life, and wealth
all beings, no longer holding them in mind
form, to enter the sphere of space
the three preceding minds, simply holding beings in mind without aversion or attachment
quiz.why: Equanimity relinquishes the three preceding states of mind while still holding beings in mind, without aversion or attachment. It does not abandon beings.

quiz.q: Why are the four minds called "immeasurable"?
options: only buddhas can cultivate them
their results cannot be measured
they take countless eons to cultivate
they pervade the ten directions equally, without division
quiz.why: Taking these four as object, the four minds pervade the ten directions equally without division, hence "immeasurable."

quiz.q: Each of the four minds removes something among beings. Which pairing is correct?
options: all four remove only craving
loving-kindness removes anger, compassion vexation, joy displeasure, equanimity aversion and attachment
loving-kindness vexation, compassion displeasure, joy anger, equanimity aversion
loving-kindness aversion, compassion anger, joy vexation, equanimity displeasure
quiz.why: Loving-kindness removes anger, compassion removes vexation, sympathetic joy removes displeasure, and equanimity removes aversion and attachment.

quiz.q: Under the general locus, where may the four immeasurable minds be cultivated?
options: only the fourth dhyāna
the four formless concentrations
the four dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna
desire-realm concentration and the not-yet-arrived state
quiz.why: The four dhyānas and the intermediate dhyāna are all places for cultivating them, as the Exegetical Treatise says. The formless realm and the desire realm are excluded.

quiz.q: Why are the immeasurable minds not cultivated in the formless realm?
options: its beings are already liberated
it has no mind or consciousness
the formless realm has no form and is unsuited to taking beings as object
its concentration is too shallow
quiz.why: Having no form, the formless realm is unsuited to taking beings as object. Shallowness is the reason given for the desire realm and the not-yet-arrived state.

quiz.q: Sharp practitioners can bring forth true understanding in the desire realm and not-yet-arrived state. Why not the immeasurable minds?
options: insight into principle is sharp enough, but the immeasurable minds are matters of practice needing deep concentration; if they arise, they belong to the first dhyāna
desire-realm beings lack loving-kindness
the Buddha forbade it
the not-yet-arrived state is already uncontaminated
quiz.why: Wisdom toward principle is sharp, so insight can arise; but supernormal powers and the immeasurable minds are practical matters that need deep concentration. When they do arise there, they belong to the first dhyāna.

quiz.q: Which of the first dhyāna's factors makes which immeasurable mind easy to arise?
options: thought: loving-kindness; joy: compassion; happiness: equanimity; one-pointedness: joy
thought and reflection hinder them all
all five aid only equanimity
initial thought and reflection: compassion; joy: sympathetic joy; happiness: loving-kindness; one-pointedness: equanimity
quiz.why: Initial thought and sustained reflection, distinguishing the desire realm, ease compassion; joy eases sympathetic joy; happiness eases loving-kindness; one-pointedness eases equanimity.

quiz.q: The fourth dhyāna and intermediate dhyāna have no joy or happiness. How can they give joy and happiness to beings?
options: the fourth dhyāna can only give equanimity
though there is none within, one takes the outward marks of joyful people as object and bestows happiness, as a desire-free practitioner still gives sense-pleasures to others
one must first drop back to the third dhyāna
the fourth dhyāna secretly has joy
quiz.why: Though without joy or happiness within, one takes the outward marks of others' joy as object, just as a practitioner free of desire may still give the finest sense-pleasures to others without being stained.

quiz.q: Under the particular locus, in which dhyāna is each immeasurable mind easiest to cultivate?
options: equanimity first, loving-kindness fourth
all four are easiest in the fourth
compassion in the first, joy in the second, loving-kindness in the third, equanimity in the fourth
loving-kindness first, compassion second, joy third, equanimity fourth
quiz.why: The first dhyāna suits compassion, the second sympathetic joy, the third loving-kindness, the fourth equanimity. Option B is the sequence the objector proposes, which the text rejects.

quiz.q: Why is compassion easiest to cultivate in the first dhyāna?
options: it is called purity of mindfulness
it contains great joy
it has happiness pervading the body
initial thought and reflection rule it, and it deeply recognizes the suffering of desire-realm beings
quiz.why: In the first dhyāna initial thought and reflection rule, deeply recognizing the suffering of desire-realm beings. Great joy is the second dhyāna, bodily happiness the third, purity of mindfulness the fourth.

quiz.q: If each stage has its own convenience, why does the Buddha say the immeasurable minds are easily attained abiding in the fourth dhyāna?
options: it is beyond the form realm
the fourth dhyāna is purity of mindfulness, the unmoving concentration, in which every merit of the Buddhadharma is easily accomplished
it has the most beings
it has the greatest joy
quiz.why: The fourth dhyāna is named purity of mindfulness and is the unmoving concentration, where every merit of the Buddhadharma is easily accomplished.

quiz.q: An objector says loving-kindness comes first and so belongs to the first dhyāna. How does the text answer?
options: the four have no order at all
the first dhyāna precedes loving-kindness by definition
this follows what fits the sense, not sequence, like answering "Śāriputra" when asked who is foremost in wisdom
it concedes the error
quiz.why: The pairing follows what is fitting to the sense, not a fixed sequence, like the ten chief disciples each foremost in one respect; asked who is foremost in wisdom, one answers Śāriputra.

quiz.q: In the Śāriputra simile, what kind of answer would be a serious error of sense?
options: refusing to answer
answering Maudgalyāyana for supernormal power
answering Śāriputra
answering by seniority in ordination when asked who is foremost in wisdom
quiz.why: Answering by seniority in ordination would be a serious error; likewise, assigning the immeasurable minds to stages mechanically by order misses the point.
